harbor_p04_001.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_001.text: The creek ferry left with a crate of chicks beneath the pilot's bench and a passenger who claimed to know every bend ahead. The pilot ignored the advice. Fen sat where she could see the bank rather than the wake. Yue kept the checked-out inquiry board inside a dry wrap and her own pack under her knees. Six copper for her ordinary return fare had been charged once to the approved ferry line. Fen held her separate ticket so tightly that its fresh ink marked her thumb.

harbor_p04_002.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_002.text: Beyond the harbor mouth, the creek narrowed between reeds bent by winter. A child on the opposite bank waved a red mitten and received a chorus from the chicks. Fen smiled at the sound, then began rehearsing what she would say to her father. The sentences grew more formal as she repeated them. Yue asked whether Luo Jian liked speeches. Fen said he fell asleep during them. She stopped rehearsing and watched the water. Neither woman pretended the journey had become easy merely because the ferry moved.

harbor_p04_003.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_003.text: At Reed Steps, the landing keeper stamped their return tickets and pointed them toward the public cookhouse collection route. Fen's overnight room had been arranged through the support clerk with a known lodging family; Yue would pay her own additional night and meal costs from personal money. The inquiry's shed lodging account was not silently extended to an inland inn. They left their packs at the confirmed house and took only the permitted forms and Fen's letter. The path rose through trees newly dark with sap.

harbor_p04_004.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_004.text: The timber camp sounded busy long before it appeared. Saw teeth rasped, a horse stamped, and somebody struck a meal pan with a ladle. The cookhouse stood outside the active cutting line. Its keeper, Aunt Jiao to everyone who ate there, recognized the collection receipt and sent a boy to tell Luo Jian his visitors had arrived. Fen planted herself beside the door with both hands behind her back. Yue stood near the table where the approved wage comparison could take place if the father still consented.

harbor_p04_005.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_005.text: Luo Jian came down the path with his right hand wrapped around two splints. He looked older than Fen's description and younger than her fear. He opened his arms, then noticed his daughter was not moving. His smile weakened. Fen asked whether he had planned to send a letter before or after he became a different man at another hiring desk. He said he had sent one. She answered that the cook had sent it when she found him. Aunt Jiao quietly took the boy back inside.

harbor_p04_006.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_006.text: For a moment, Yue thought the reunion might fail before anyone sat down. Then Luo Jian said the cook was right to write and he had been wrong to wait. Fen stared at his splints. She asked whether the fingers would remain crooked. He said the clinician had not promised a final shape yet. He could use the hand lightly after another review. Fen made a small sound between anger and a sob. He held out his uninjured hand without insisting she take it. She finally did.

harbor_p04_007.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_007.text: They sat on a bench whose legs had been shortened unevenly. Luo Jian tried to explain the camp work, the lost days after the creek delay, and his worry that the harbor wage would be held too long. Fen kept returning to the silence. Yue excused herself to buy tea while they spoke. The inquiry appointment had brought her to a permitted contact point. It did not entitle her to hear the family's whole reckoning. Aunt Jiao gave her a cup so hot she had to leave it on the counter.

harbor_p04_008.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_008.text: The cook said Luo Jian had hidden the injury until supper because he did not want to lose a shift. She had seen blood on the bench and called ordinary care. Yue asked whether that account could be recorded if he wanted it for a separate claim. Jiao agreed, adding that the camp foreman already had his own accident report. The harbor's voyage wage inquiry could not adjudicate camp injury. Yue kept the lead in her personal notes with permission and waited for Luo Jian to request anything further.

harbor_p04_009.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_009.text: When Fen called Yue back, her father had agreed to the contract comparison. He inspected the witnessed copy found in the shipboard chest and confirmed it matched his voyage terms. He identified the earlier payment and explained the two hiring name orders. Yue read the resulting statement aloud before he signed with his uninjured hand. He wanted the remaining harbor wages paid to himself through a collection route he could use. Fen did not become his recipient because she had carried the ticket through every week of waiting.

harbor_p04_010.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_010.text: The request would return to Qin Shuo for decision under the established wage process. Luo Jian also wanted the commercial clerk to permit Fen to collect the cleared chest on his behalf, if no competing property claim remained. That was a separate written authorization identifying the objects and collection terms. Yue asked him to read both purposes before signing. He laughed, sadly, and said his daughter had become better at keeping papers than he was. Fen answered that somebody had needed to keep the things he left behind.

harbor_p04_011.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_011.text: The statement complete, Luo Jian invited them to see the camp's safe visitor path. He could not show them the active saw line without the foreman's permission. Fen wanted to know where he had been sleeping; he chose to show her the shared bunk room himself. Yue remained outside while they looked. The camp was neither the secret prison Fen had imagined nor the comfortable retreat He Ming had feared. It was rough paid work, with ordinary rules, several neglected repairs, and people trying to save enough to go elsewhere.

harbor_p04_012.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_012.text: Luo Jian intended to return to the harbor after the clinician's next review. He could travel with a splinted hand if his ordinary care instructions allowed it, but he did not want to risk the crowded ferry without checking. Fen asked why he could not simply come now. He showed her the review appointment, which fell the following morning. She decided to stay until then within her confirmed lodging arrangement. Yue would remain too, paying her own expenses. The return fare did not need changing because the ticket allowed that interval.

harbor_p04_013.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_013.text: Their lodging host served millet soup and described the creek as though it were a difficult cousin. The water had moved one landing stair every spring for twenty years, he said, and people kept acting surprised. Fen asked whether he knew her father before this week. He did not. That answer pleased her more than a comforting guess would have. Yue washed her own bowl and sat by the small stove. The checked-out forms rested in their dry wrap, ready to return. The family had another night to speak.

harbor_p04_014.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_014.text: During the night, Fen woke Yue because she thought she heard the saws running. The sound came from a loose shutter in the wind. They secured it with the host's ordinary peg and went back to bed. Fen remained awake. She said she had wanted her father's return so fiercely that she had not thought about having to live with him afterward. Yue said return did not remove everything that happened during absence. Fen asked whether she was allowed to stay angry after embracing him. Yue said she could choose her own pace.

harbor_p04_015.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_015.text: At the care room the following morning, the clinician removed the outer bandage and checked Luo Jian's fingers. He permitted ordinary travel with protection and rest, while restricting gripping and heavy work. The final degree of recovery remained uncertain. Luo Jian accepted a written card. Fen read it without touching the dressing. Yue waited outside and heard neither medical details nor private questions. When they emerged, father and daughter had agreed to return together on the afternoon ferry. The timber camp's work account would follow through its separate process.

harbor_p04_016.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_016.text: The camp foreman met them at the cookhouse before departure. He gave Luo Jian the existing injury report reference and a written wage calculation for camp shifts completed. Luo questioned one date and received a corrected copy after the shift sheet was checked. The foreman did not ask Fen to sign away a future injury claim in exchange for payment. Yue watched from the public table. She had no reason to turn every employer into the same adversary. This man had a neglected work bench to explain and several immediate acts he could do correctly.

harbor_p04_017.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_017.text: On their way to collect the packs, a horse cart blocked the path beside a stack of squared beams. The driver tried to reverse without a clear view. Luo Jian stepped toward the wheel by habit, then stopped when Fen caught his good sleeve. The foreman sent an ordinary ground guide and cleared the visitor path. Yue moved back with them. The moment ended without accident or spectacle. Fen looked at her father's wrapped hand and said she expected him to keep it long enough for the doctor to inspect it again.

harbor_p04_018.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_018.text: The return ferry carried fewer passengers and no chicks. Luo Jian sat with his injured hand supported as the ordinary care card directed. Fen took the bank side and held his chest authorization in the same cloth as her ticket. Yue kept the inquiry statement separate from personal letters. The pilot steered past the new channel marker without asking anybody's cultivation rank. Along the reeds, small buds had opened since yesterday. Fen noticed them and asked her father whether he knew the name of the tree. He said he knew the timber price.

harbor_p04_019.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_019.text: Back at the harbor, the support clerk recorded Fen's return and closed the particular contact search after confirming its result with her. The wage claim remained open pending the custodian's decision. The property authorization went to the commercial desk. Luo Jian's current lodging arrangement stayed private unless he chose otherwise. Fen carried him to the tea seller's table in the sense of directing every step, not lifting his body. He obeyed with a tired smile. The tea seller charged them for soup and refused to treat reunion as payment.

harbor_p04_020.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_020.text: Yue returned the loaned inquiry board and all checked-out forms that evening. Han Pei counted pages, recorded custody, and filed Luo Jian's signed statement under its existing reference. The ferry expense remained six copper, leaving eighteen of the original twenty-four ceiling. Yue's private lodging and meals at Reed Steps appeared nowhere on that expense line. She slept deeply after the journey, then woke irritated by the gulls. A successful search had not transformed her into somebody who enjoyed being awakened before dawn by noisy ordinary birds.

harbor_p04_021.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_021.text: He Ming came to meet Luo Jian at the tea stall the next morning. She had known him for years at the packing lane, where he always announced a wage increase that never arrived. He told the same joke with his splinted hand on the table. She laughed, then scolded him for making Fen wait. He accepted the scolding longer than he might have before. Fen listened while washing bowls nearby. Hearing another adult say her anger was reasonable mattered more than the advice everyone had given her while her father was missing.

harbor_p04_022.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_022.text: Luo Jian wanted to leave the camp account behind and begin harbor work as soon as he could. The clinician's restriction made his usual loading task unavailable. Han Pei showed him the ordinary job board and warned that a public wage correction was not medical fitness for every job. A bookbinder sought someone to sort paper offcuts one-handed at a low table. Luo disliked the rate but inspected the task. Fen said paper would make a useful change from carrying everything that could break his fingers. He decided to ask.

harbor_p04_023.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_023.text: At the binder's shop, the owner paid for a short trial and let Luo stop when his supported hand ached. Yue heard about it later from Fen, who was delighted by how seriously her father described different paper weights. He had never asked what her own bowl-washing shifts required. Now he asked to watch one. She told him customers did not want a man staring at their soup. They agreed he could help stack clean bowls after the stall closed if the tea seller wanted ordinary assistance.

harbor_p04_024.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_024.text: Fen took her father to the shore wall on his first free evening. She showed him the scale where she had called names and the sheltered corner where He Ming repaired her ticket's cloth. Luo Jian listened without defending the silence again. At the tea stall, he had been able to joke about returning. Here, every place held a day his daughter had spent waiting. He said he had imagined keeping worry away from her. Fen answered that he had only kept the information away.

harbor_p04_025.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_025.text: They passed the repair shed while Yue was mending her boot. Luo asked whether he could help with the needle, then remembered his restricted hand. Fen took the thread instead and complained about the knot. Yue let them argue over it. The father knew an old sailor's stitch; the daughter knew the sole needed a different angle. Their disagreement found something small enough to finish. When the repaired boot stood on the floor, Luo said he would like to learn where Fen wanted to work next.

harbor_p04_026.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_026.text: The question made Fen suspicious. She expected him to guide her toward a choice he had already made. He admitted he wanted them nearer Willow Reach, then said that was his wish rather than her answer. She described the tea seller's plans for another stall and the binder's offer to teach clean copying. Neither was a promise of a grand life. Both had grown while he was gone. Luo looked at the boot, flexed his uninjured hand, and asked whether she would show him the second stall tomorrow.

harbor_p04_027.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_027.text: The harbor inquiry now had a person behind Luo Jian's held wage amount, but three other recipient questions remained unresolved. One involved a crew worker who had died after leaving the vessel, according to a report from a neighboring care house. Another involved a woman who did not want her former partner told where she lived. The third involved two claimants disputing whether a payment recipient had been named before departure. Yue reported each as a separate question. Locating a body, protecting a living address, and interpreting an appointment needed different evidence.

harbor_p04_028.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_028.text: Dai Min asked to speak privately at the north office. The deceased worker was her husband, though she had not accepted the report until the care house supplied its identification record and personal effects description. Han Pei referred the representative and estate questions to the proper household desk. The wage obligation could be calculated from the contract while payment waited for a lawful recipient. Dai did not have to describe her marriage at the public queue. She sat beside the closed cabinet and cried quietly, furious at the ordinary furniture for looking unchanged.

harbor_p04_029.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_029.text: Yue asked whether Dai wanted someone with her. The woman said she wanted everyone to leave, then asked Yue to remain by the door. Yue did, saying nothing for several minutes. Dai's husband had survived the voyage and died of an ordinary illness on shore. His death was not evidence that the quarantined hold carried disease. Sui Yan's public findings would continue to stand on tests and relevant medical reports. The offices needed accurate boundaries. Dai needed somebody willing to let the silence be longer than a clerk's customary pause.

harbor_p04_030.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_030.text: The care house sent verified copies through authorized custody after Dai consented to the relevant request. Its record identified admission, treatment, death, and the basis of identity. The household desk would decide who could receive his remaining wages, considering any other entitled person and giving the required notice. Qin kept the held amount protected in the bond claim schedule. Yue could help explain the forms, but neither sympathy nor a marriage description would substitute for that decision. Dai took the receipt and asked whether the care house still had his ordinary comb.

harbor_p04_031.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_031.text: The comb had been retained with his effects. Dai chose to request its return through the appropriate collection route. She said he had bought it after someone teased him about arriving ashore looking like a storm rope. The story broke her composure again. Yue felt the inadequacy of every useful task she knew. She could locate a receipt, preserve a claim, and carry a permitted question. None would put the comb back in the living man's hand. She stayed by the door until Dai decided to go home.

harbor_p04_032.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_032.text: The protected-address claimant came to the office under the name on her own contract, accompanied by a support worker she had chosen. Her former partner had filed a household inquiry describing her as missing. She was alive, wanted her earned wages, and did not want a reunion. Han Pei verified her identity privately and recorded her own chosen collection route. The former partner could receive the lawful status of his request without being given her address. Yue met the woman only within the permission she supplied for wage explanation.

harbor_p04_033.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_033.text: He Ming objected when she heard, through the public status line, that one household contact search had ended without reunion. She feared somebody could use privacy to leave a parent hungry. Yue asked whose obligation had been established in that file. He Ming knew none. The woman was not He Jun. The question stung, and He Ming walked away. Later, she returned to say she had borrowed another family's story because she was still angry at her brother. Yue accepted the admission without asking to hear more private details.

harbor_p04_034.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_034.text: The dispute over a named wage recipient proved less dramatic and more stubborn. A crew worker had sent a message asking his cousin to collect. The cousin held a copy; the worker's current reply named his wife instead. The old copy did not say whether the appointment could be revoked. Qin sought the worker's verified current instruction and gave both proposed recipients notice of the question. Nobody would be paid twice. Yue helped locate the delivery dates, which mattered without making the cousin a liar for arriving with an older page.

harbor_p04_035.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_035.text: While those questions proceeded, the merchant challenged two working days in the supported two-hundred-twenty-four remainder. Han Pei produced the shift sheets and the relevant foreman's account. One disputed day was confirmed. The second was supported by a delayed unloading tally and claimant testimony after the signed sheet had been damaged. Qin explained his evidentiary conclusion in writing after hearing the response. The earned total remained six hundred forty-two. No new money was added merely because an argument consumed another afternoon. The records justified the amount already claimed.

harbor_p04_036.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_036.text: Miao left the hearing with his employer's challenge rejected and his own notebook full of expenses. Yue found him outside turning a coin between his fingers. He said she seemed to enjoy showing where a merchant was wrong. She answered that he had been right about counting earlier payments, and wrong about counting the loan receipt as wages. He said people remembered the wrong part. Yue thought of Han Pei's heading and Yan Su's brace. They stood in the same uncomfortable harbor, whether they admitted that kinship or not.

harbor_p04_037.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_037.text: The agent said his employer had promised him a share of recovered bond money. He had not been told the voyage's unpaid wage total when he accepted the job. That gave him a reason to favor release but did not prove he had hidden the packet. Yue asked whether he wanted the statement recorded for the inquiry. He said no, then yes for the employment term alone, if its document could be produced. She told him to send it to the relevant desk. Their conversation was not an official finding.

harbor_p04_038.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_038.text: At the quay, Yan Su replaced the inspection cover on the repaired platform with a removable fitting. The carpenter and keeper approved the design after ordinary load checks. Future inspection would expose the sheltered brace face instead of trusting what could be seen from the lane. Deren, now on a paid seated task, watched and gave unwelcome advice about the screw heads. The carpenter found two of his comments useful. Deren announced that he expected royalties. Bo offered him a bent nail, and the crew laughed.

harbor_p04_039.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_039.text: Yue spent a free afternoon helping the repair shed's boy repaint the fish kite. Its patched paper had begun to curl, so they used a thin brace and less paint. He wanted to add four luminous arms to the fish. Yue said an ordinary fish already had serious difficulties owning the sea. He said extra arms would help it sign documents. Han Pei arrived with tea and endorsed the argument. They gave the fish four absurd fins instead. Its legal ambitions grew while its weight stayed within the ordinary kite's lift.

harbor_p04_040.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_040.text: He Ming's mother reached the harbor during the sixth week on an ordinary passenger boat. He Ming met her at the landing with the room she had paid from her own wages already ready. He Jun came too, carrying no grand apology. Their mother looked at his coat and said the pocket repair was crooked. Then she embraced him. He Ming laughed so suddenly that the older woman asked what was funny. Nothing, she said, which was not true but was the answer she could give without reopening every letter at the quay.

harbor_p04_041.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_041.text: Yue met the older woman over supper. She was smaller than He Ming and spoke as though each ordinary object had been placed incorrectly by someone who ought to know better. She admired the spoon recovered from the hold and asked why He Jun had not used it every day. He Ming answered that they were still asking several questions of him. The older woman said questions should wait until food was served. He Jun grinned. He Ming rolled her eyes, and the family looked briefly like people who had practiced living together.

harbor_p04_042.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_042.text: After supper, He Ming walked Yue back to the shed. She said her mother had decided to stay for a month, which meant the room arrangement would need another payment. He Ming could cover it now without borrowing from He Jun. The wage did not cure the quarrel. It changed how much the quarrel cost her. She wanted the other households to have that freedom too. Yue asked whether she still wished to act as delegate where people specifically chose her. The woman said yes, and fewer speeches would be welcome.

harbor_p04_043.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_043.text: Han Pei paid the next completed inquiry shifts under the existing forty-eight-copper wage line. By the end of six weeks, twelve half-days had been completed and twenty-four copper of Yue's total wage allowance earned. The office meal and bed account continued at the agreed term rate. Copying and outreach expenses remained separately receipted, with no transfer from claimant wages. Yue put part of her own pay toward a repaired boot sole. She was halfway through the appointment and no closer to a secret rank, merely better supplied for ordinary walking.

harbor_p04_044.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_044.text: The permit review returned its first source comparison. The old yard hiring clerk had listed workers as yard housed to avoid seeking individual lodging details before departure. A separate note proposed using that status for permit accounting, though the actual fees and authority still needed review. The findings did not automatically impose a debt on every worker in the list. The permit desk asked the former clerk and yard owner for their accounts. Han Pei corrected current contact fields using verified sources, keeping the old entries in the history.

harbor_p04_045.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_045.text: The former clerk answered from another town. He said the yard owner had instructed the batch address method and that individual slips would follow in the packet. He denied knowing the packet traveled aboard. The owner denied directing any permit misclassification but admitted approving the shortened departure summary. Their statements conflicted on one act and agreed on another. Yue arranged the relevant source pages for the authorized review, resisting a story with only one convenient culprit. The workers' wage claims remained protected while the offices considered responsibility.

harbor_p04_046.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_046.text: Sui Yan's handling crew found another problem in the lower hold: several tubs had shifted against a partition, leaving a passage narrower than the plan required. Nobody entered to pull them aside by hand. Yan Su proposed a revised ordinary tackle route from the repaired higher walkway. The captain asked for a fresh work plan, keeper checks, and a way to stop if the partition moved. The delay angered everyone who had believed the first clearance notice meant all physical difficulty was finished. It angered Sui Yan too.

harbor_p04_047.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_047.text: That evening, the captain admitted her own impatience to Yue while they walked the duty path. She wanted the vessel cleared before the new seasonal arrivals crowded the berth. She had a performance review in another month. Pressure did not need a malicious merchant to exist. Sometimes it arrived as a reasonable calendar and a colleague asking why the harbor still looked unfinished. Yue asked who could review the revised handling plan independently. Sui Yan named a licensed keeper from the south berth and sent the request before going home.

harbor_p04_048.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_048.text: The independent keeper came the next morning and rejected one proposed anchor position. It would draw the load toward a weakened partition face. Yan Su revised the tackle route and thanked her, though he sounded tired. Yue watched ordinary expertise correct ordinary expertise. Her qi arms did not enter the plan. They could guide a light marker during a dry check if separately agreed, but the loaded tubs demanded rated rigging and trained crew. The harbor's useful power existed in many places where no luminous hands appeared.

harbor_p04_049.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_049.text: The revised dry check used an empty marked container and stopped before any hazardous handling. Yue took the offered light-marker task only after checking her reserve and the agreed limit. Her fourth-stage control held steady for the brief interval. She withdrew, rested, and logged the small use in her practice notes. The foreman recorded the alignment result in the work file, without claiming her cultivation guaranteed the later loaded task. That afternoon, she declined a second practice request because her shoulders were tired. No one lost wages for accepting her answer.

harbor_p04_050.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_050.text: At the north office, Dai Min received the household desk's recipient decision after the required notices and source checks. It authorized her to collect the identified remaining wage claim under the stated basis, leaving unrelated estate questions outside the payment. She read the reasons with the support worker she had chosen. Yue waited at the public table to explain the calculation if asked. Dai asked only whether the receipt would carry her husband's full name. Han Pei showed it to her. The old shortened line remained linked in the record.

harbor_p04_051.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_051.text: The protected-address claimant collected through her chosen route. Her former partner received a limited status reply that did not disclose her whereabouts. The crew worker in the appointment dispute supplied verified current instructions, and the custodian resolved the recipient question after considering both pages and the notice responses. Those decisions completed the remaining two hundred twenty-four copper in supported wages. Actual collections were recorded as they occurred. The three payment groups now totaled one hundred fifty-four, one hundred sixty-eight, and two hundred twenty-four: five hundred forty-six paid from the guarantee bond.

harbor_p04_052.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_052.text: Qin's bond ledger showed two hundred fourteen copper remaining from the original seven hundred sixty. That remainder did not become a general repair fund. The merchant could request its return under the guarantee rule after the remaining notice and review conditions were met. Identified unresolved claims, if any arose within the proper route, would be handled by their own evidence. Yue checked the public aggregate statement with Han Pei. Wages earned totaled six hundred forty-two, including the ninety-six paid earlier and five hundred forty-six now paid. The arithmetic finally closed without closing every life.

harbor_p04_053.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_053.text: Luo Jian used part of his voyage wage to repay the tea seller for meals Fen had received beyond her bowl-washing arrangement. The seller showed the actual account instead of naming a rounded favor. Fen insisted on keeping the wages she had earned. Her father agreed. He asked whether she wanted to return to Willow Reach when his hand improved. She said she wanted to think about work in the harbor. The answer startled him. His daughter's waiting weeks had become part of a life he could not simply carry home.

harbor_p04_054.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_054.text: He Ming helped Dai Min collect the comb from the care-house effects packet. The item returned under recorded authorization, wrapped in a cloth that had belonged to her husband. The woman held it at her doorway while gulls screamed over the roofs. He Ming asked whether she wanted company. Dai said not tonight. She thanked her and shut the door. He Ming walked back slowly. She had spent weeks demanding a reunion and now understood how fortunate it was to have somebody available to quarrel with at supper.

harbor_p04_055.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_055.text: The wage list at the north office changed status after the last supported collections. Han Pei dated the aggregate update and kept the earlier public notices in the record. Thirteen household references had produced several workers' claims, not thirteen identical missing persons. One contact search had found a man deliberately elsewhere, another had led to an injured father, another protected a woman's chosen separation, and one family faced a confirmed death. The office could say what had happened without claiming every interrupted household had become whole.

harbor_p04_056.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_056.text: Yue expected the completed wage total to release her from the harbor's central work. Instead, the administrator asked what the remaining six weeks of her inquiry appointment could usefully do. She would not take a second wage payment for the same shifts or expand her powers. The unresolved task was to document how bad contact information traveled and propose a workable future route, while limited property outreach continued under the existing scope. Han Pei wanted that work. He Ming feared another pile of pages would replace the relief already paid.

harbor_p04_057.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_057.text: They met at the tea seller's table after hours to argue about it. He Ming said people needed somewhere they could ask a long question without surrendering a day's pay. Han Pei said a permanent chair outside the office would need assigned time and a keeper who could answer. Yan Su said workers also needed a way to report unsafe pressure before injury, which was another responsibility altogether. Yue asked each to describe one actual day when the missing task hurt. The conversation became less abstract and more difficult.

harbor_p04_058.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_058.text: Han Pei described the morning she left a queue to search a restricted cabinet, returning to find half the people gone to their shifts. He Ming described carrying three slips between offices while paying for her mother to wait elsewhere. Yan Su described a boy afraid to call stop because the merchant threatened his next hiring. They did not merge those failures into a single slogan. They began with different stories and sought places where a durable arrangement could carry some of the burden ordinary kindness had been bearing.

harbor_p04_059.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_059.text: The captain joined them late, still smelling faintly of clean lime. She said the harbor needed a public explanation of what quarantine did and where other questions belonged, but she would not promise her office could answer all of them. He Ming groaned at another boundary. Sui Yan accepted the groan and asked what sentence would have saved her the first wrong walk. The woman thought, then offered a plain one. Han Pei wrote it on a scrap. For once, an official phrase began in the mouth of the person who had been sent elsewhere.

harbor_p04_060.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_060.text: The conversation ended without a plan or an appropriation. That restraint disappointed Yue more than she expected. She had hoped the paid wages would lead naturally to a shared next step. Instead, people carried different wounds and priorities away from the same table. She went back to the repair shed and found the fish kite hanging from a nail. Its four ridiculous fins had dried unevenly. She turned it so the morning light would reach both sides, then laughed at herself for trying to improve another object after midnight.

harbor_p04_061.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_061.text: A newly arrived ship agent came to Sui Yan's shed carrying a petition signed by three merchants who wanted the Salt Lantern berth freed immediately. The captain read it before answering. They could ask the administrator to review delay and resources; they could not direct hazardous cargo into an unapproved lane. She gave the planned handling date and the outstanding technical questions. After he left, she sat very still. Yue had never seen her look so tired. Being right about a boundary did not make the pressure harmless.

harbor_p04_062.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_062.text: Sui Yan went home before another letter arrived, leaving the ordinary duty keeper in charge as the roster allowed. Yue met her the next morning carrying a loaf baked by her inland son's recipe. It had collapsed at the center. The captain blamed a harbor oven, then conceded she had forgotten one step. They ate the ugly slices beside the path. Yue liked the way the failure annoyed her without threatening her whole character. Sui said her son would insist on hearing exactly which step. Some reviews could be welcome.

harbor_p04_063.speaker: narrator
harbor_p04_063.text: The seventh week began with a southbound vessel waiting outside the berth and a revised cargo-handling plan ready for its final ordinary checks. The wage bond balance stood at two hundred fourteen. Yue's inquiry term had six weeks left, with twelve paid half-days completed. No final institutional reform had been approved. The cargo title disputes remained active, and the permit review still needed its reasoned findings. Spring had moved fully into the harbor, bringing more boats, more work, and less room to postpone a question merely because the winter version of it had been difficult.
